facts.claim: The Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence
facts.context: Congress voted for independence on July 2 and approved the text of the Declaration on July 4, 1776.
facts.goDeeper: John Adams expected July 2 to be the date Americans celebrated forever. He was off by two days.

facts.claim: The battles of Lexington and Concord began the Revolutionary War
facts.context: British troops marching to seize colonial arms met militia at Lexington on April 19, 1775.
facts.goDeeper: No one knows who fired the first shot on Lexington Green, and both sides insisted it was the other.

facts.claim: Cornwallis surrendered his army at Yorktown
facts.context: Trapped by American and French troops and a French fleet, Cornwallis surrendered on October 19, 1781.
facts.goDeeper: The French navy, not the Continental Army, was the decisive factor: it sealed off Cornwallis's only escape route by sea.

facts.claim: The Treaty of Paris formally ended the Revolutionary War
facts.context: Signed September 3, 1783, the treaty recognized American independence and set the new nation's borders.
facts.goDeeper: Fighting had effectively stopped two years earlier at Yorktown, but the negotiations dragged on through 1782 and 1783.

facts.claim: The Boston Tea Party took place
facts.context: On December 16, 1773 colonists dumped 342 chests of East India Company tea into Boston Harbor.
facts.goDeeper: The protest was partly against a tax cut: the Tea Act actually made British tea cheaper, which threatened colonial smugglers.

facts.claim: The Boston Massacre occurred
facts.context: British soldiers fired into a hostile crowd on March 5, 1770, killing five men.
facts.goDeeper: John Adams defended the accused soldiers in court, and most were acquitted. He later called it one of his finest services to his country.

facts.claim: Number of men who signed the Declaration of Independence
facts.context: Fifty-six delegates signed, most of them on August 2, 1776, not July 4.
facts.goDeeper: The youngest signer was 26 and the oldest, Benjamin Franklin, was 70.

source.title: Signing of the United States Declaration of Independence

facts.claim: Parliament passed the Stamp Act
facts.context: The 1765 tax on printed materials triggered the first coordinated colonial resistance and was repealed the following year.
facts.goDeeper: The phrase 'no taxation without representation' came out of this fight, a decade before any shots were fired.

facts.claim: George Washington took command of the Continental Army
facts.context: Congress appointed Washington in June 1775 and he took command outside Boston in July.
facts.goDeeper: He refused a salary, asking only that his expenses be covered. The final bill came to a sum that raised eyebrows in Congress.

source.title: George Washington in the American Revolution

facts.claim: Washington crossed the Delaware and attacked Trenton
facts.context: The crossing happened on the night of December 25-26, 1776, and the surprise attack captured most of a Hessian garrison.
facts.goDeeper: The famous painting of the crossing was made 75 years later by a German artist and gets almost every detail wrong, including the flag.

facts.claim: The American victory at Saratoga convinced France to join the war
facts.context: Burgoyne surrendered his army in October 1777; France signed a formal alliance the following February.
facts.goDeeper: Benedict Arnold was one of the heroes of Saratoga, three years before he turned traitor.

facts.claim: The Continental Army began its winter encampment at Valley Forge
facts.context: The army arrived in December 1777 and stayed until June 1778.
facts.goDeeper: Roughly 2,000 men died there, almost all from disease rather than cold or starvation.

facts.claim: The United States Constitution was signed in Philadelphia
facts.context: Thirty-nine delegates signed on September 17, 1787, after a summer of debate.
facts.goDeeper: The Constitution replaced the Articles of Confederation, under which the country had no president, no national courts and no power to tax.

facts.claim: George Washington was inaugurated as the first president
facts.context: Washington took the oath in New York City on April 30, 1789.
facts.goDeeper: He was elected unanimously by the Electoral College, the only president ever to manage it, and then did it again in 1792.

facts.claim: The Bill of Rights was ratified
facts.context: The first ten amendments took effect December 15, 1791.
facts.goDeeper: Twelve amendments were sent to the states. One of the two rejected then was finally ratified in 1992, 203 years later.

facts.claim: Thomas Paine published Common Sense
facts.context: The pamphlet appeared in January 1776 and argued for outright independence rather than reconciliation.
facts.goDeeper: It sold in the hundreds of thousands in a country of about 2.5 million people, making it proportionally one of the best-selling American books ever.

facts.claim: Number of colonies that declared independence
facts.context: Thirteen British colonies on the Atlantic coast joined the Declaration.
facts.goDeeper: Britain had other North American colonies, including Quebec, Nova Scotia and the Floridas, that stayed loyal.

facts.claim: All the delegates signed the Declaration of Independence together on July 4, 1776
facts.context: The text was approved on July 4, but the famous engrossed copy was not signed until August 2, and a few delegates signed even later.
facts.goDeeper: The document most Americans picture, with Hancock's oversized signature, was written out on parchment weeks after the vote.

source.title: Signing of the United States Declaration of Independence

facts.claim: Paul Revere rode through the countryside shouting 'The British are coming!'
facts.context: The ride was meant to be discreet, with British patrols on the roads. The colonists also still considered themselves British, so the warning was about 'the regulars.'
facts.goDeeper: Revere was captured that night and never reached Concord. Two other riders, William Dawes and Samuel Prescott, carried the alarm onward.

facts.claim: Benedict Arnold was a successful American general before he switched sides
facts.context: Arnold was one of the ablest field commanders of the early war, badly wounded at Saratoga, before plotting to hand West Point to the British in 1780.
facts.goDeeper: There is a monument at Saratoga to Arnold's wounded leg, deliberately unnamed, because his leg served the country honorably even if the rest of him did not.
